title: Ἔχις καὶ ῥίνη
part: The Viper and the File (Chambry 116 · Perry 93)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 116 (= Perry 93). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἔχις εἰσελθὼν εἰς χαλκουργοῦ ἐργαστήριον παρὰ τῶν σκευῶν ἔρανον ᾔτει· λαβὼν δὲ παρ’ αὐτῶν ἧκε πρὸς τὴν ῥίνην καὶ αὐτὴν παρεκάλει δοῦναί τι αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr: Echis eiselthōn eis chalkourgou ergastērion para tōn skeuōn eranon ēitei· labōn de par’ autōn hēke pros tēn rhinēn kai autēn parekalei dounai ti autōi.
sentences.l: A viper, having entered into a coppersmith's workshop, kept asking a contribution from the tools; and having got something from them he came to the file and kept calling on her to give him something.
sentences.i: A viper got into a coppersmith's workshop and went round begging a contribution from the tools; and when he had got something from them, he came to the file and pressed her to give him something too.
sentences.n: ἔρανος is not alms but a club-contribution: the sum friends put together to help one of their number, repayable in kind. The viper is going round the workshop putting in for one. ᾔτει and παρεκάλει are imperfects of repeated asking — he worked his way along the bench. ῥίνη is feminine, so the file is 'she' throughout, and the relative ἥτις in her reply confirms it.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ὑποτυχοῦσα εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ εὐηθὴς εἶ παρ’ ἐμοῦ τι ἀποίσεσθαι οἰόμενος, ἥτις οὐ διδόναι, ἀλλὰ λαμβάνειν παρὰ πάντων εἴωθα. »
sentences.tr: Hē de hypotychousa eipen· « All’ euēthēs ei par’ emou ti apoisesthai oiomenos, hētis ou didonai, alla lambanein para pantōn eiōtha. »
sentences.l: And she, taking-up-the-word, said: « But you are simple, thinking you will carry off something from me, I who am accustomed not to give but to take from everyone. »
sentences.i: The file took up the word and said: « You are a fool to think you will carry anything off from me, when it is my way not to give to anyone but to take from everyone. »
sentences.n: ὑποτυχοῦσα is the regular fable word for cutting in with an answer — 'taking-up-the-word', not seizing anything. εὐήθης is literally 'of good character' (εὖ + ἦθος), but in Attic the word has slid to 'simple, easily taken in': the file is calling the viper a fool. ἥτις introduces a relative clause with a first-person verb (εἴωθα), the speaker classing herself: 'I, being the sort who…'. εἴωθα is a perfect with present force, 'I am in the habit'.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι μάταιοί εἰσιν οἱ παρὰ φιλαργύρων τι κερδανεῖν προσδοκῶντες.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti mataioi eisin hoi para philargyrōn ti kerdanein prosdokōntes.
sentences.l: The story shows that those who expect to gain something from money-lovers are wasting their effort.
sentences.i: The story shows that anyone who expects to get something out of a miser hopes in vain.
sentences.n: μάταιος of a person is not 'stupid' but 'to no purpose' — the man's expectation is empty, so he is. φιλάργυρος is literally 'silver-loving'.
